Gloria Steinem, feminist icon, dies at 92

Gloria Steinem, a journalist, activist, and organizer who became the most recognizable face of the U.S. women's movement, died at 92. Steinem resisted being cast as feminism's singular face, but for six decades she carried its ideas into mainstream America across its second and third waves. She made the personal political: an illegal abortion at 22 preceded decades of fighting first to legalize abortion and then to defend that right. Steinem died peacefully, surrounded by people who loved her at her home in New York City, according to a Thursday announcement posted from her and her foundation's Instagram accounts. "Gloria's greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard," the announcement said.

Steinem first drew national attention as a journalist in 1963 when she went undercover as a Playboy Bunny and exposed the job's low pay and sexist treatment. Soon, she was both chronicling feminism's emerging second wave and organizing within it. She co-founded Ms. magazine, bringing feminist arguments about work, sex, politics, family, and reproductive rights to a mass audience. She also helped found the National Women's Political Caucus. She took her fight to Congress, testifying for the Equal Rights Amendment in 1970, and to the American people, campaigning for its ratification.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire attributes Steinem's normalization of feminism to her appearance and media presence, contrasting her with earlier feminists like Kate Millett, Angela Davis, and Betty Friedan, whom it describes as "angry, cantankerous, and mentally ill." The Daily Wire also claims Steinem said she would have been "stopped there" if she had had a child as a young single woman, a claim not present in other accounts. The Daily Wire attributes this quote to a 2022 interview with Meghan Markle and Vogue magazine. The Slate article mentions Steinem's abortion in 1957 and her doctor's influence, but does not include the claim about having a child. The Axios article notes Steinem's abortion at 22 and her later activism around abortion rights, but does not mention the 2022 quote. The BBC and NPR accounts focus on her early life, activism, and legacy without the specific claims about her personal life or the 2022 interview.

Sources BBC · The Daily Wire · NPR · Axios · The Dispatch · Slate

Trading food for medicine and crossing the river by zip line are part of life in Nepal flood zone

Survivors in Nepal’s flood-affected areas are facing severe shortages of essential medicines, with some resorting to selling relief food to afford their prescriptions. Suresh Kumar Karanjit, a resident of a relief center in Devighat, Nuwakot district, described the lack of medicine for his heart condition, stating he sold a carton of noodles he received as relief for 400 rupees ($2.60) to buy his regular medication. The floods, triggered by a glacier collapse on Aug. 26, devastated towns and valleys, destroying homes, roads, bridges, and critical infrastructure. Nepal’s disaster chief, Dharam Raj Uprety, noted that health camps with doctors and medicine have been set up at each relief center, while authorities are also focusing on hygiene and sanitation to prevent disease.

Rescue efforts have focused on hydropower tunnels where workers are believed to have survived for over a week. Two workers were rescued alive from the Trishuli 3A tunnel nine days after the disaster, with one, Sanjay Shah, describing his ordeal of trying to save others before being trapped. Officials confirmed the rescue of Sanjay Shah and Kabir Maharjan, with Maharjan in critical condition. Nepal’s Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina expressed hope that more workers will be rescued. The death toll has risen to at least 1,259, with over 5,000 people missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

Where the accounts differ

The Associated Press and Washington Examiner both report that at least 1,259 people were killed, while Al Jazeera and ABC News state the death toll is at least 1,287. The Guardian and ABC News mention 1,287 deaths, with the Guardian also noting that 5,000 people remain missing. The Washington Examiner and Associated Press report that China said 21 people were killed and 541 missing on the Tibet side, while Al Jazeera and ABC News state that China reported 16 additional deaths and 546 missing people, bringing the total to 1,268 and 4,762 missing on both sides. The Guardian and ABC News also mention that more than 5,000 people remain missing, while the Associated Press and Washington Examiner report over 5,000 missing.

Sources Associated Press · Al Jazeera · BBC · The Guardian · ABC News · Washington Examiner

Iran fires on its Gulf neighbors, retaliating for U.S. strikes after a monthlong lull

Iran launched missile and drone attacks on U.S. allies in the Gulf on Wednesday, following a night of American bombardment that included a strike on a wedding party in southern Iran. The six-month conflict has led to rising oil prices and economic instability. The U.S. military struck Iranian military targets, including air defense sites and maritime assets, in response to Iranian attacks on commercial shipping and American forces in the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian officials claimed the U.S. strike killed four people, including two children, at a wedding in Kuhestak, while the U.S. denied targeting civilians. The strikes marked the end of a monthlong lull in fighting.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and BBC both report that the U.S. strike killed four people, including two children, at a wedding in Kuhestak. Al Jazeera and BBC also mention that the attack may constitute a war crime. NPR and Christian Science Monitor report that the U.S. strike hit a home hosting a wedding, while BBC and Al Jazeera specify that the attack occurred at a home in Kuhestak. Christian Science Monitor and FOX News mention that the U.S. strike targeted Iranian military assets, including mine-laying capabilities and communications sites, while NPR and BBC do not specify these targets. FOX News and Straight Arrow News report that the conflict began on February 28, 2026, with Operation Epic Fury, while other accounts do not mention this date or operation.

Sources NPR · BBC · Al Jazeera · Christian Science Monitor · Straight Arrow News · FOX News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump names new acting Army secretary after Driscoll resigns

President Trump on Thursday named Adam Telle, a civilian leader in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, as the acting Army secretary, following the resignation of Dan Driscoll earlier this week. Telle is currently the assistant secretary of the Army for civil works. Driscoll resigned as the Army's top civilian leader this week, following months of behind-the-scenes friction with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Driscoll had drawn up plans to transform the Army's operations but shared concerns with the Trump administration that Hegseth had pushed out some of the generals responsible for implementing those plans.

Telle will now oversee the nation's largest fighting force at a time when the U.S. is still engaged in conflict with Iran and significant Army forces are stationed in the Middle East. The war has contributed to the U.S. military's shortfall in critical weapons like the Patriot and THAAD defense missile interceptor systems, which are operated by the Army. Democrats and Republicans lamented Driscoll's departure, with some blaming Hegseth directly. Sen. Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican who is retiring and sometimes has clashed with Trump, said on social media that Hegseth "is creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks."

Where the accounts differ

CBS News reports that Driscoll resigned after months of friction with Hegseth and that Hegseth asked Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George to step down in April. FOX News and Al Jazeera also mention the tensions between Hegseth and Driscoll, but FOX News adds that Tillis called for Trump to replace Hegseth, while Al Jazeera highlights Hegseth's broader controversies, including the "Signalgate" incident. The Guardian and CBS News note that Driscoll did not provide a reason for his resignation, while Newsweek states Driscoll gave no explanation for his departure. CBS News and The Guardian mention that Driscoll was an ally of Vice President JD Vance, while FOX News and Al Jazeera attribute Tillis's criticism of Hegseth to his own political stance.

Sources CBS News · Newsweek · FOX News · Al Jazeera · BBC · The Guardian

Russia’s strikes near Moldova raise alarm over Putin’s plans for Europe’s eastern flank

Russia has intensified strikes against Ukrainian-Moldovan border infrastructure, according to Moldova’s national security advisor Stanislav Secrieru, who told Fox News Digital. These strikes are aimed at disrupting Ukraine’s grain exports through Moldova, which has become a key transit route for Ukrainian grain to Romanian ports. Moldova cut rail transit tariffs by half to maintain the flow of exports. The Moldovan government has also reported multiple violations of its airspace by Russian drones and missiles, with 17 incidents recorded in August 2025. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy recently visited Moldova to express solidarity with President Maia Sandu amid the escalating tensions.

The European Union and NATO have responded to recent Russian actions, including a suspected drone attack on a cargo plane in Germany’s Leipzig airport. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte have warned that Russia is growing increasingly reckless and called for a stronger response. Germany has blamed Russia for the attack and announced sanctions, including the closure of Russian cultural institutions, which Russia has retaliated by closing its own Goethe-Institut centers in Russia.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that Moldova has recorded 17 Russian airspace violations in August 2025, while the Christian Science Monitor and The Guardian do not mention specific numbers of violations. The Guardian and BBC attribute the Leipzig drone attack to Russia, while the BBC adds details about the suspects identified in the attack, including a Belarusian with a Russian passport and another with Latvian and Russian passports. The Guardian also notes that the attack was linked to Russia’s hybrid warfare tactics, a point not explicitly made in the other accounts. The Christian Science Monitor mentions that Russia is suspected of paying local gangs to carry out sabotage, a claim not made by the other outlets.

Sources FOX News · BBC · Christian Science Monitor · The Guardian · NPR · ABC News

Biden-appointed judge blocks Trump’s latest birthright citizenship executive order

A federal judge has temporarily blocked President Donald Trump’s latest attempt to restrict birthright citizenship, citing the Supreme Court’s prior ruling that children born in the U.S. to parents who are unlawfully present are citizens at birth. The order, issued in August 2026, sought to deny automatic citizenship to children of “alien enemies” and those engaged in “birth tourism.” Judge Deborah Boardman, a Biden appointee, issued a preliminary injunction against the executive order, arguing it was “almost certainly unconstitutional” as it contradicted the Supreme Court’s decision in *Barbara v. Trump*. The White House criticized the ruling, calling it an example of “activist judges” attempting to block Trump’s “commonsense agenda.”

The executive order aimed to limit birthright citizenship for children of foreign government employees and those whose parents are deemed “alien enemies,” including members of designated terrorist organizations. The order also targeted “birth tourism,” the practice of traveling to the U.S. to give birth for citizenship. The Supreme Court had previously ruled that children of undocumented immigrants and temporary visitors are citizens at birth, but allowed for exceptions such as foreign diplomats and during hostile occupations.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that the judge cited the Supreme Court’s June ruling in *Barbara v. Trump* and that the White House called the ruling an “activist judge appointed by Biden attempting to thwart President Trump’s commonsense agenda.” The New York Post states that the judge cited the same ruling and that the White House spokesperson said the order was “consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court.” The Federalist adds that the judge previously gave a lenient sentence to the attempted killer of Justice Kavanaugh and that Rep. Chip Roy introduced impeachment articles against her. The Guardian and BBC both note that the judge cited the Supreme Court’s June ruling and that the government has not yet issued guidelines on how to implement the restrictions. Straight Arrow News mentions that the judge initially denied an injunction due to the complaint referencing the 2025 order, which had already been struck down.

Sources FOX News · New York Post · The Federalist · The Guardian · BBC · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

ICE officer faces federal charges for lying over shooting of Venezuelan immigrant

Federal prosecutors have charged an ICE officer, Christian Castro, with making false statements to investigators about the shooting of a Venezuelan immigrant, Julio Sosa-Celis, in Minnesota in January. The charges are part of a broader investigation into the incident, which occurred during the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in Minneapolis known as Operation Metro Surge. Castro was initially accused of shooting Sosa-Celis in the leg through a closed door, but surveillance footage contradicted his account of the incident. The Justice Department initially charged Sosa-Celis with assault, but later dropped those charges after acknowledging that officers involved made untruthful statements. Castro is also facing state-level assault charges in Minnesota.

The shooting has sparked controversy, with Sosa-Celis's attorney criticizing the federal charges as insufficient, arguing that Castro lied to cover up the shooting without self-defense justification. Minnesota officials have sought to extradite Castro from Texas, but Texas Governor Greg Abbott refused to sign the extradition request, citing Castro's return to Texas for work. A federal judge ruled against Minnesota's request to keep Castro in jail pending extradition, allowing him to be released.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and The Guardian both report that the Justice Department initially charged Sosa-Celis with assault, which was later dropped after acknowledging untruthful statements by officers. The Daily Wire and CBS News mention that the charges against Sosa-Celis were dismissed with prejudice in February, citing newly discovered evidence. The Washington Examiner and The Guardian note that the federal charges against Castro were blocked by Justice Department officials, while NPR and The Daily Wire state that the federal charges are separate from the state charges. The Guardian and BBC mention that the Trump administration launched Operation Metro Surge in early December 2025, while NPR and CBS News refer to it as occurring earlier in the year.

Sources NPR · Washington Examiner · The Guardian · BBC · The Daily Wire · CBS News

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: One sentence naming the concrete consequence that earns the slot: "Trump's legal challenge to USPS mail voting rules threatens to disenfranchise millions of voters, undermining election access and integrity."

Trump asks Supreme Court to lift block on USPS plan to restrict mail voting

The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to lift a block on the U.S. Postal Service plan to restrict mail-in voting for the midterm election. Key parts of the plan are currently blocked by a temporary restraining order from a federal judge in Boston. North Carolina is scheduled to start mailing out absentee ballots on Friday, which officially kicks off the voting season for this year's midterms. Election officials have stated that ballots will be mailed out as expected, and they are prepared to administer a secure election even if the new limits go forward.

The USPS plan requires states to submit lists of eligible voters to the Postal Service through an online portal and include specific design elements on mail ballot envelopes, such as barcodes. The plan was issued in response to a March executive order by President Trump, who claimed it was to stop illegal voting by non-U.S. citizens. However, many studies and audits show that such voting is rare. The Supreme Court previously ruled on a procedural question about one of the lawsuits but has not yet ruled on the legality of the order or the USPS plan.

Where the accounts differ

NPR states that the USPS plan has not directly changed mail-in voting for the midterms and that key parts are blocked by a court order. ABC News reports that the USPS plan includes requirements for states to submit lists of eligible voters to the Postal Service through an online portal and that the plan has been held up by multiple lawsuits. CBS News adds that election officials warn the new requirements would be difficult, if not impossible, to implement in time for the midterms. Straight Arrow News mentions that the Supreme Court ruled a lawsuit against the order was filed prematurely and that the Postal Service posted changes to its website, leading to a new lawsuit. Washington Examiner notes that the Supreme Court lifted a lower court order blocking an executive order instructing federal agencies to develop policies regarding mail ballots. Just The News states that the Supreme Court previously ruled the administration could move forward with the executive order but did not rule on its legality.

Sources NPR · ABC News · CBS News · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · Just The News

No source labeled left covered this story.

U.S. and Venezuela Reach Oil Agreement with U.S. Gaining Control of 65 Billion Barrels

The Trump administration announced a deal granting the U.S. majority control over 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s oil reserves, with the U.S. government acquiring a 35% equity stake in North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), a private oil company led by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt López. Under the agreement, the U.S. will have the right to purchase 20% of the oil produced by NABEP at the cost of production, while the remaining 80% can be sold to other buyers. The deal also gives the U.S. government veto power over NABEP’s board of directors, requiring a majority of board members to be U.S. citizens. Venezuela’s interim government granted NABEP 100-year rights over 17 oil fields, and the U.S. plans to use the oil to refill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which has reached historically low levels. Venezuela’s president, Delcy Rodríguez, publicly supported the deal, claiming it could generate over $200 billion in tax revenue for the country.

Chevron announced a separate $7 billion investment to expand its oil production in Venezuela, aiming to increase output to 600,000 barrels per day by 2031. The company has been granted access to two additional oil fields in Venezuela’s Orinoco Belt, which contains vast reserves of extra-heavy crude. Chevron’s CEO, Mike Wirth, stated the investment reflects confidence in Venezuela’s resource potential and its ability to attract investment. The deal with NABEP is part of a broader U.S. strategy to boost oil production and lower gas prices, with Trump claiming the agreement would “substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans, long into the future.”

Where the accounts differ

Fox Business reports that the U.S. government received a 35% ownership stake in NABEP’s parent company through the Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital, while The Guardian and Axios describe the same stake as being held by the Pentagon. The Daily Wire states that Chevron’s investment is part of the broader agreement with NABEP, while CBS News and Axios note that Chevron’s investment is separate from the Trump administration’s deal with NABEP. The Guardian and Axios mention that Betancourt has been investigated by U.S., Swiss, and Spanish authorities over alleged money laundering, while Fox Business and The Daily Wire provide more detail on the nature of the investigations and Betancourt’s denial of wrongdoing. The Daily Wire and Axios report that Betancourt was listed as an unnamed “conspirator” in a 2018 federal indictment, while Fox Business and The Guardian do not mention this specific charge.

Sources Fox Business · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · CBS News · Axios · Straight Arrow News

Two dead and three officers injured in Minneapolis shooting

A shooting occurred in downtown Minneapolis on Wednesday, resulting in two fatalities and three injured police officers. The suspect was killed, according to multiple outlets. The incident took place near 15 E. Grant St., specifically at Loring Towers, a high-rise apartment building. Officers were involved in a prolonged response, including the use of long guns and armored vehicles. Several individuals were taken to the hospital, with at least one person dying at the scene. The Minnesota governor and other officials expressed support for law enforcement and condolences for the victims.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and FOX News differ on the number of fatalities, with the Examiner reporting two dead and FOX News stating three. The Washington Examiner and Newsweek also differ on the number of injured, with the Examiner reporting at least five others injured and Newsweek stating five others wounded. The Daily Wire and CBS News both report that the suspect died, but the Daily Wire mentions that the suspect's death was reported as suicide, while CBS News states it was a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The FOX News and Just The News differ on the number of injured officers, with FOX News reporting four others injured and Just The News stating three officers were injured. The Newsweek account provides additional details about the suspect, Carlton Johnson II, including his eviction status and alleged threats, which are not mentioned in other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · CBS News · FOX News · Just The News · Newsweek

Lindsay Clancy's murder trial deadlocked after five days of deliberations

Lindsay Clancy, 36, faces three counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children, found strangled at their home in January 2023. A jury of nine women and three men has been deliberating for five days, with jurors reporting they remain deadlocked. Judge William Sullivan gave them a Tuey-Rodriguez charge to continue deliberations. Clancy has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, citing postpartum psychosis. Her defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, said she is emotionally unable to handle another trial. A woman, Dawn Light, 56, was arrested for allegedly filming jurors outside the courthouse, though she claims she was only trying to take a photo of Clancy.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that retired judge Jack Lu claims social media has shifted the conventional wisdom about retrials, favoring the defense now due to its influence. The Daily Wire characterizes the jurors as part of a "deranged TikTok mob" and criticizes the defense's narrative as a "mass psychosis" rooted in "narcissism" and "feminism." The Federalist references historical cases like Constance Fisher's drownings in the 1950s and ties the current case to "feminist victimhood dogma" and "therapeutic culture." The Guardian and BBC both report on Dawn Light's arrest for filming jurors, with the Guardian noting the judge's order prohibiting such actions. The New York Post adds that Light was arrested around 3:40 p.m. and that the jury requested dismissal at 3:30 p.m. on Tuesday.

Sources FOX News · The Daily Wire · The Federalist · The Guardian · BBC · New York Post

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

USS Lincoln crew hits the streets of Thai beach city after lengthy Middle East deployment

The USS Abraham Lincoln, a U.S. aircraft carrier, arrived in Pattaya, Thailand, after a record-setting deployment to the Middle East. The ship, which has been at sea for over 260 days, is expected to stay in Thailand for several days before continuing its journey back to the U.S. Crew members disembarked at Laem Chabang port, with some heading to Pattaya, a popular destination for U.S. troops. Vendors and travel agents gathered near the Hard Rock Hotel, offering souvenirs and services to the arriving sailors. The ship’s deployment included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 260 days, with the total deployment lasting 286 days. The Navy has acknowledged concerns about mental health and food shortages but has downplayed the severity of the issues.

The Lincoln’s arrival in Thailand has drawn attention due to its long deployment and the potential impact on the local economy. Pattaya, a city known for its nightlife and tourism, has increased security measures around the area. Local officials estimate the visit could bring in around $3 million for the tourism-dependent city. The ship’s stop is part of a larger U.S. military operation in the Middle East, with the Lincoln having been diverted from its original Pacific route due to the war with Iran. The ship is expected to depart Thailand this weekend.

Where the accounts differ

The Associated Press and The Guardian differ on the exact duration of the Lincoln’s uninterrupted time at sea, with AP reporting 264 days and The Guardian stating 270 days. The Guardian also mentions reports of attempted suicides on the ship, which the Associated Press does not include. The Daily Wire and Newsweek both report that the Lincoln has spent over 260 days at sea, but Newsweek adds that the deployment has prompted calls for investigations into deteriorating conditions and mental health concerns. The Guardian and BBC differ on the exact number of days at sea, with the Guardian stating 270 days and the BBC reporting 250 days. The Daily Wire and The Guardian both mention the presence of sex workers in Pattaya, but the Guardian provides more context about the city’s history with U.S. troops and its transformation into a nightlife hub.

Sources Associated Press · Straight Arrow News · The Guardian · Newsweek · BBC · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Apple changes name of Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ in maps app

Apple has updated the label for Lake Ontario to “Lake America” in its maps app for U.S. users, following an executive order from President Donald Trump. The change occurred on Tuesday, the same day John Ternus became Apple’s new CEO. Apple is now the second U.S.-based tech giant to comply with Trump’s order, following Google, which also changed the name for U.S. users. The U.S. Geographic Names Information System, which standardizes federal naming conventions, was cited by both companies as the basis for the change. Canadian users continue to see “Lake Ontario,” while international users may see both names. MapQuest, another map provider, has refused to change the name, stating it will not comply with Trump’s request.

The renaming of Lake Ontario is part of Trump’s broader effort to assert U.S. influence over naming conventions, including renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America” and changing the name of Denali to “Mount McKinley.” Trump’s order does not compel private companies to change their naming conventions, but it does update the U.S. government’s official reference guide. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum stated that Trump “reached out to Apple directly” to request the change, though Apple did not immediately comment on the matter.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The Guardian both state that Trump “reached out to Apple directly” to request the name change, while Axios and Just The News attribute the claim to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. Al Jazeera and The Guardian mention that Trump’s order does not compel private companies to change their naming conventions, whereas Axios and The Guardian also note that Trump’s order does not compel Canada to change the name. The Guardian and Axios clarify that Canadian officials have stated they will not call Lake Ontario “Lake America,” while Al Jazeera and The Guardian do not explicitly state this.

Sources Al Jazeera · Axios · BBC · Just The News · The Guardian

No source labeled right covered this story.

Trump to speak on both nights of midterm convention in programming shuffle: Report

President Donald Trump is now scheduled to speak on both nights of the Republican Party’s 2026 midterm convention next week, according to a report. The event in Dallas is set to mark the first midterm convention of its kind, highlighting the administration’s crackdown on fraud, tax cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and increased access to healthcare through TrumpRx. The convention’s opening night will coincide with a Super Bowl rematch between the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks. On Thursday night, the convention is set again to compete with viewers due to an NFL rivalry matchup between the San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams in Melbourne, Australia. Several major networks, including CBS and CNN, are not expected to cover a majority of the two-day convention live starting Sept. 9 in Dallas.

President Trump vowed Wednesday to campaign for Republicans in 35 competitive races during the final month before the midterm elections. He promised to hold telephone town halls in support of embattled candidates, saying that they “work amazingly.” Trump specifically noted that he will be campaigning on behalf of congressional candidates, but not gubernatorial ones. He also pledged to travel to Texas to campaign for Senate candidate Ken Paxton, before joking: “You might not like the way he dresses.” Trump also plans to travel to Alaska and stump for GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The New York Post both report that Trump will speak on both nights of the convention, while The Daily Wire and Newsweek focus on Trump’s campaign strategy for the midterms. The Washington Examiner mentions the convention’s opening night coinciding with a Super Bowl rematch, while The New York Post and Newsweek do not. The Daily Wire and The New York Post both report that Trump will campaign in 35 races, while The Washington Examiner and Newsweek do not mention the number of races. The Daily Wire and The New York Post both report that Trump will hold telephone town halls, while The Washington Examiner and Newsweek do not. The Daily Wire and The New York Post both report that Trump will campaign in Texas for Ken Paxton, while The Washington Examiner and Newsweek do not.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · CBS News · New York Post · Newsweek · The Daily Caller

No source labeled left covered this story.

NBA suspends Clippers owner Ballmer, fines team $30M, Kawhi Leonard $700K in cap circumvention case

The NBA announced on Wednesday that Los Angeles Clippers owner Steve Ballmer has been suspended for one year and the team fined $30 million for violating salary cap circumvention rules. Kawhi Leonard was fined $700,000 for his role in the case. The league cited the Clippers for improperly funneling off-court endorsement and income opportunities to Leonard through corporate partners, including Aspiration, Boingo Wireless, Daktronics, and Lockton Insurance. The investigation, which began in September 2025, was prompted by a report from podcast journalist Pablo Torre about a $28 million endorsement contract between Leonard and Aspiration Fund Adviser LLC, a company that filed for bankruptcy last year. The Clippers had previously denied wrongdoing and stated they would challenge the findings. Leonard, through his new agent, expressed regret for the distraction caused by the situation and accepted responsibility for lapses in judgment by people within his inner circle.

The NBA also suspended President of Basketball Operations Lawrence Frank for six months and team president of business operations Gillian Zucker for one year. The league accused Ballmer of failing to create conditions under which his organization abided by the NBA’s circumvention rules. Leonard’s trade to the Toronto Raptors, which had been on hold pending the investigation, is now expected to proceed, with both teams indicating they are moving forward with the deal.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and The Guardian both mention that the Clippers had said they would challenge the findings, while BBC and Al Jazeera include the Clippers’ statement about the investigation being "heavily biased" and "predetermined narrative." The Guardian and Al Jazeera note that the investigation was conducted by Wachtell Lipton, a New York law firm, while NPR and BBC do not specify the law firm. The Guardian and Al Jazeera also mention that the NBA’s investigation found a "pattern of misconduct" and that the Clippers were a "prior offender" of salary cap circumvention rules, which are not explicitly stated in NPR, Newsweek, or BBC. Just The News does not mention the investigation being conducted by a law firm or the Clippers being a prior offender.

Sources NPR · Newsweek · Just The News · The Guardian · Al Jazeera · BBC

No source labeled right covered this story.

Warnings Over Coast Guard Jet Surfaced Before Mullin Emergency Landing

A Coast Guard plane carrying Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin made an emergency landing after losing an engine on Wednesday. The C-37A aircraft, a military version of a Gulfstream V, landed safely at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport with 14 people on board and no injuries reported. Mullin confirmed the landing on X, stating the pilots handled the situation "feel routine" with "no panic, just straight professionalism." The pilot reported losing the right engine and requested an emergency landing, according to an audio recording. The incident occurred as the plane was traveling from Georgia to Washington, D.C.

Prior concerns about the aircraft's age were raised by the Department of Homeland Security, which flagged the plane for obsolescence issues. In 2025, DHS stated the C-37A was "22 years old and faces significant avionics and communications obsolescence issues," which could impact its availability for critical missions. The plane is one of two long-range command and control aircraft used by the Coast Guard to transport senior officials, including the DHS secretary.

Where the accounts differ

Newsweek and The Daily Wire both mention the C-37A is the military version of a Gulfstream V, while FOX News and New York Post refer to it as a C101. The Daily Wire and Newsweek state the plane entered Coast Guard service in 2002, while FOX News and New York Post do not specify the service entry date. The Daily Wire and Newsweek note the plane was flagged for obsolescence in 2025, while FOX News and New York Post refer to it as being flagged "last year." The Daily Wire and Newsweek mention the plane was 22 years old, while New York Post and FOX News refer to it as 23 years old. The Daily Wire and Newsweek attribute the obsolescence concerns to DHS, while FOX News and New York Post attribute it to the Coast Guard.

Sources Newsweek · Just The News · FOX News · New York Post · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-left or left covered this story.

The brief ends here.
